solution: For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\), \(\text{adj}(A)\) swaps the diagonal entries and negates the off-diagonal ones, giving \(\begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). Matching \(\begin{bmatrix} 4 & a \\ -3 & b \end{bmatrix}\) gives \(a = -2,\ b = 1\) — option A.

For \(\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), \(|A| = -1\) and \(\text{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{-1}\,\text{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), the matrix itself — option B.
Since \(A(\text{adj}\,A) = |A|\,I = kI\), we have \(k = |A|\). For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(|A| = 1 - 4 = -3\) — option D.
For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -4 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(\text{adj}(A)\) swaps the diagonal and negates the off-diagonal entries: \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\) — option B.
\(A^{-1}\) fails to exist when \(|A| = 0\). For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} \lambda & 1 \\ -1 & -\lambda \end{bmatrix}\), \(|A| = -\lambda^2 + 1 = 0 \Rightarrow \lambda = \pm 1\) — option B.
This is a rotation matrix (orthogonal, \(|A| = 1\)), so \(A^{-1} = A^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\alpha & \sin\alpha \\ -\sin\alpha & \cos\alpha \end{bmatrix}\) — option B.
\(F(\alpha)\) is a rotation about the z-axis, so its inverse is the rotation by \(-\alpha\): \([F(\alpha)]^{-1} = F(-\alpha)\) — option A.
\(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) swaps rows 1 and 2, and applying it twice restores the identity, so \(A^2 = I\) and \(A^{-1} = A\) — option B.
If \(A\) is symmetric then \((A^{-1})^{T} = (A^{T})^{-1} = A^{-1}\), so \(A^{-1}\) is also symmetric — option A.
Since \(A(\text{adj}\,A) = |A|\,I\), and here it equals \(\begin{bmatrix} 10 & 0 \\ 0 & 10 \end{bmatrix} = 10\,I\), we get \(|A| = 10\) — option B.
